summaries.example: Imagine a red apple. You can study it as a thing that reflects light, or as something you see and taste. Neutral monism asks whether both ways of talking might come from one more basic kind of reality. That basic reality would not be mental, like a thought, and would not be material, like an object. It would be neutral. Different groups of neutral parts could then make up the apple and your experience of it.
summaries.summary: Neutral monism is a theory about what reality is ultimately made of. “Monism” means that the most basic reality is one kind of thing. “Neutral” means that this basic thing is neither mental nor material by itself. Minds and physical objects might be formed from the same neutral ingredients, arranged or connected in different ways. For example, one group of ingredients may count as a brain, while another organization of them may count as a thought or feeling. Different philosophers have suggested different candidates for the neutral ingredients, including parts of experience, events, or information. The theory tries to solve the mind-body problem: the puzzle of how thoughts and experiences relate to bodies and brains. Its supporters value its simple, unified picture. Its critics ask whether it can really explain consciousness, perception, mistakes, and the difference between mental and physical things.
key_ideas: Neutral monism says that the deepest level of reality has one basic kind of ingredient.
Mind and matter may be different groupings or arrangements of the same neutral ingredients.
The view was developed in different ways by thinkers such as Ernst Mach, William James, and Bertrand Russell.
A major challenge is explaining how neutral ingredients can produce real thoughts and experiences without simply becoming mental or material.
summaries.why_it_matters: Neutral monism matters because it offers a third choice in a famous debate. Instead of saying that everything is mind, or everything is matter, it looks for something more basic than both. This can help us think about how science studies brains and how people experience the world. It also shows why a simple theory may still face difficult questions: explaining experience is not easy, even when all parts of reality are connected.

important_terms.definition: The view that everything most basic in reality is one kind of thing, rather than two completely different kinds.
A basic thing that is not, in itself, mental or material, but can help make up both.
Things connected with thoughts, feelings, seeing, remembering, or having experiences.
Things studied as objects, bodies, events, or processes in the physical world.

questions_to_think_about: Could one thing be described in both a mental way and a material way?
What makes a thought different from a physical object?
If experiences are made from neutral ingredients, what gives them their special feeling?
Would a simpler picture of reality always be a better one?

summaries.example: Consider seeing a red tomato. A naïve realist might say that the red feature you experience is simply part of the tomato. A physicalist might treat the experience as wholly grounded in physical brain activity. A neutral monist instead asks whether both the tomato and the experience can be constructed from, or grounded in, more basic entities that are intrinsically neither mental nor physical. On a Jamesian approach, the same portion of experience can function as an object in one network of relations and as a mental episode in another. Russell’s approach is different: he emphasizes neutral events and the constructions that physics and psychology make from them.
summaries.summary: Neutral monism is a monistic metaphysics designed in large part to address the mind-body problem. It claims that ultimate reality has a neutral intrinsic nature: its basic constituents are not mental and not physical, even though mental and physical entities may be formed from them or grounded in them. This position must clarify both terms in its name. Neutrality may mean that basic entities are neither mental nor material, that they can belong to mental and physical groups, that both kinds of laws apply to them, or—in a different proposal—that they are intrinsically both. The entry argues that these interpretations should not be run together, since the Both View can make neutral monism resemble panpsychism or dual-aspect theory. Monism also need not mean that only one concrete object exists; most versions accept many basic entities and several levels of reality. Mach treats elements of experience as neutral and explains mental and physical objects through functional groupings. James uses “pure experience,” which becomes subject or object according to its relations and practical role. Russell develops a system of neutral events and logical constructions, while distinguishing the abstract structure described by physics from the intrinsic qualities known in experience. The theory is attractive for its parsimony and its promise to connect psychology, physics, and perception. Yet critics question whether its base is really neutral, whether mental or physical entities are merely eliminated, and whether experience can emerge from non-experiential constituents. Contemporary proposals appeal to information, complex basic entities, or Russellian monism, but remain disputed.
key_ideas: Neutral monism differs from idealism and materialism by denying that the basic nature of reality is fundamentally mental or fundamentally material.
The entry distinguishes several accounts of neutrality, including the Neither View, the Both View, and accounts based on actual or possible constitution and laws.
Most versions are pluralist in practice: they posit many basic neutral entities and allow higher-level mental and physical entities to be derivative.
Mach emphasizes neutral elements, James emphasizes pure experience and its functional groupings, and Russell emphasizes events and logical constructions.
The view promises parsimony, a bridge between perception and physics, and a unified account of scientific inquiry.
Objections include the possibility that the theory secretly becomes mentalism, physicalism, dual-aspect theory, or phenomenalism, and the difficulty of explaining conscious experience.
summaries.why_it_matters: Neutral monism matters because it tests whether the apparent divide between mind and matter is fundamental. It offers an alternative to idealism, materialism, and dualism by placing both mental and physical descriptions at a derivative level. The theory also raises a central methodological issue: a framework can be economical and scientifically unifying while still needing a convincing account of consciousness, perception, and error. Its modern versions keep these questions active in metaphysics of mind.

important_terms.definition: The metaphysical view that ultimate reality has one basic kind, while minds and material things are derivative or organized groupings.
The claim that a basic entity is intrinsically neither mental nor physical. Other versions define neutrality by its roles or relations.
A relation in which something depends on, or is constituted by, something more fundamental without necessarily being identical to it.
The philosophical puzzle of explaining the relation between conscious experience and physical bodies or brains.
A method associated especially with Russell in which complex structures of known entities take the place of inferred entities.
The qualitative character of an experience, such as how red or pain feels, considered apart from its representational or causal role.

questions_to_think_about: Is being intrinsically neither mental nor physical a genuine description, or only a refusal to choose between two descriptions?
Can mental and physical properties be derivative from neutral entities without being eliminated?
Does explaining consciousness through causal-functional organization adequately explain experience itself?
Does Russell’s distinction between physical structure and intrinsic quality support neutral monism, or move toward physicalism?
Should informational states, qualities, events, or something else serve as the neutral basis?

summaries.example: Suppose two students look at the same red backpack. One describes its color as a feature of an object that reflects light. The other describes seeing red as a personal experience. Neutral monism asks whether the object and the experience could be made from the same basic neutral elements, with their different meanings coming from how those elements are connected. William James would stress that one part of experience can count as the thing seen in one setting and as the seeing of it in another. Bertrand Russell instead gives a more scientific picture, in which neutral events are organized into physical systems and mental episodes.
summaries.summary: Neutral monism is a metaphysical theory about the basic structure of reality. It combines monism—the claim that ultimate reality has one fundamental kind—with neutrality—the claim that this kind is not intrinsically mental or physical. Mental and material things can still exist, but they are usually understood as higher-level groupings, arrangements, or products of neutral entities. The entry separates several meanings of neutrality. The most distinctive is the Neither View, according to which a basic entity is intrinsically neither mental nor physical. Other proposals define neutrality by whether an entity can belong to both mental and physical groups, is governed by both kinds of laws, or is intrinsically both. The last proposal can make neutral monism difficult to distinguish from dual-aspect theories or panpsychism. Neutral monists also disagree about monism itself: it may concern one concrete thing, one basic kind, or one deepest level of reality. Traditional figures illustrate different strategies. Ernst Mach describes neutral elements that become physical or psychological parts depending on their functional connections. William James uses pure experience and argues that subject and object can be different roles played by one continuous field. Bertrand Russell treats neutral events as materials for logical constructions and argues that physics gives us structural knowledge while leaving intrinsic qualities less fully described. The theory is attractive because it reduces the number of basic categories and may connect perception, psychology, and physics. However, critics ask whether it eliminates ordinary mental and physical entities, disguises a form of materialism or mentalism, or can explain conscious experience from neutral components. key_ideas: Neutral monism is not the claim that there is only one object; it usually allows many neutral entities arranged in levels.
The Neither View says basic entities are neither mental nor physical, while the Both View says they are both; these lead toward different theories.
Mach, James, and Russell all connect mind and matter to neutral constituents, but they describe those constituents and their organization differently.
The theory aims to avoid the difficulty of explaining how two fundamentally different substances—mind and matter—interact.
Critics worry that neutral monism may reduce mental and physical things away, or secretly turn into idealism, physicalism, panpsychism, or dualism.
Newer versions explore information, qualities, and intrinsic features of matter, but the source presents their success as unsettled.
summaries.why_it_matters: Neutral monism matters because it offers a way to reconsider a familiar either-or choice: perhaps reality is not fundamentally mind or matter. The view encourages careful attention to how we define “mental,” “physical,” “basic,” and “neutral.” It also connects philosophical questions about consciousness with questions about perception, science, and the limits of physical description. Even if one rejects it, examining its strengths and objections clarifies the mind-body problem.

important_terms.definition: A theory saying that reality is ultimately based on one kind of neutral entity, while minds and material things arise from its organization.
The idea that a basic entity is neither mental nor physical in its own intrinsic nature; some philosophers propose different tests for neutrality.
The view that only one fundamental kind of reality exists, though it may contain many entities and levels.
The relation by which higher-level things depend on more basic things or arrangements.
The problem of explaining how conscious minds and physical bodies are related.
A group or pattern of basic entities that can play the role of a more complex thing, such as a body or a belief.

questions_to_think_about: Is a neutral entity genuinely a third kind, or merely a physical or mental entity described in a different way?
If a brain and a thought are arrangements of the same elements, what explains their different roles?
Can a theory preserve the reality of minds while treating them as derivative?
Why might Russell distinguish the structure described by physics from the qualities known in perception?
Does a simpler theory of reality necessarily give a better explanation of consciousness?
